name: Pagination
intent: Return a large list in small pages, in a way that stays fast and stays correct while the data changes underneath.
scenario: A feed API returns the newest posts first. A client loads page after page while new posts keep arriving at the top.
problem: A list of millions of rows cannot be returned in one response: it is slow, uses too much memory and wastes bandwidth. Splitting it into pages is easy to do wrongly. The obvious approach, 'skip N rows', gets slower with every page and shows duplicates or skips items when the data changes between requests.

howItWorks.title: Offset pagination: skip N, take M
howItWorks.text: The client sends page=3&limit=20, and the server runs something like OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20. It is simple and allows jumping to any page. But the database must walk past all the skipped rows, so deep pages are slow, and if rows are inserted or deleted between requests the pages shift.

howItWorks.title: Why offsets drift
howItWorks.text: If a new item arrives at the top while you are on page 1, everything moves down by one. Page 2 then starts with the item that was last on page 1, so you see a duplicate. If an item is deleted, one item slides across the boundary and is never shown.

howItWorks.title: Cursor (keyset) pagination: continue after the last thing seen
howItWorks.text: Each response includes a cursor that encodes the last item's sort key, for example its id or timestamp. The next request asks for 'items older than this'. The query uses an index to jump straight to that position, so every page costs the same, and new or deleted items elsewhere do not shift the page.

howItWorks.title: Make the cursor opaque and the order total
howItWorks.text: Return the cursor as an opaque string (often base64 of the key), so clients do not build their own. The sort must be unique and stable: if sorting by timestamp, add the id as a tie-breaker, or rows with equal timestamps can be skipped or repeated.

howItWorks.title: Tell the client when there is more
howItWorks.text: Return the items, a next cursor, and whether more pages exist. Cap the page size on the server. Total counts are expensive on large tables, so provide them only if the product really needs them, or as an approximate number.

pros: Cursor pagination has constant cost per page and no drift
Offset pagination is simple and supports page numbers and jumping
Protects the database from huge queries
cons: Offset gets slower with depth and shows duplicates or gaps when data changes
Cursors cannot jump to page 50 or show 'page 3 of 80'
Cursor needs a stable, indexed, unique sort order
Both need a server-side cap on page size
whenToUse: Offset for small, stable lists, admin tables and UIs that need page numbers
Cursor for feeds, logs, large or fast-changing data and infinite scroll
Any list endpoint that can grow without a known bound
whenNotToUse: Cursor when users must jump to an arbitrary page and the data is small enough for offset
Returning the whole list when it is genuinely small and bounded
pitfalls: Offset on a huge table, so page 10,000 takes seconds
Sorting by a non-unique column without a tie-breaker
Letting clients request any limit, including a million
Cursors that expose internal ids or let clients tamper with the query

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Asks for a page and remembers where it stopped.

roles.label: API
roles.description: Turns offset or cursor into a bounded query.

roles.description: Walks or seeks to the right position.
